cim: House Advances Bill to Track Artificial Intelligence in Jobs
cim_eredeti: House Advances Bill to Track Artificial Intelligence in Jobs
szoveg_eredeti:
The AWARE Act (H.R. 9381), a bill directing the federal government to measure how artificial intelligence is used in the workplace, has been placed on the House Union Calendar and is eligible for floor consideration. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the measure, which would direct the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to collect and report the data. No floor vote has been scheduled, leaving lobbyists and congressional staff tracking workforce and AI policy without a date for the next legislative action. ​

The bill is a measurement proposal. It would amend the 1913 law establishing the Department of Labor to require federal labor statistics to include AI use, workplace conditions, and productivity. BLS would have to begin collecting the data within 18 months of enactment.

The bill identifies gaps in existing data on employer adoption of AI, worker-level use, changes to job tasks, training needs and effects on hiring, wages and employment. It says existing BLS surveys do not adequately capture those developments. Policymakers, employers, workers, educators and researchers are among the groups that could benefit from the information. The measure would not directly regulate employers or AI developers.

The House Education and Workforce Committee held a markup June 25 and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a 19-14 vote. It was reported Nov. 18 as H. Rept. 119-887 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 782. The bill has no cosponsors from either party. The committee's markup record covers 11 bills, and the transcript shows Walberg offered a substitute amendment before the chair moved to report the bill.

Walberg chairs the committee. Bloomberg Law reported June 29 that the legislation would direct BLS to study AI's effects on the workforce.

The objection centers on duplication and funding. At the markup, the committee's ranking member, Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA), argued that other agencies already perform much of this work, citing the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, and that the bill provides no additional funding for BLS. The legislation was reported as amended, and the reported version retains the requirement to begin collecting statistics within 18 months.

Republicans argue that better data on artificial intelligence's impact on the workforce is essential to shaping effective policy. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI), announcing the legislation on June 22, said, "We must have information about its impact" as AI transforms the workplace. The House Education and Workforce Committee echoed that position, saying the bill would help generate data to "support workers, inform policy, and keep America competitive."

Democrats have raised concerns that the legislation would duplicate existing federal research without providing additional resources. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA), the committee's ranking member, argued that the bill would burden the "already underfunded BLS" with responsibilities "largely already being performed by other agencies." He warned that the measure "will force BLS to conduct duplicative work" and urged lawmakers to oppose it.

The bill's reach is narrow: It would establish a federal data-collection requirement without directly imposing new rules on employers. The dispute centers on agency resources and potential overlap with existing surveys. Obstacles include the 19-14 committee vote, the lack of cosponsors, and Scott's funding objection. Next developments to watch include the House floor schedule and any Rules Committee notice on H.R. 9381.
